'''Ellery Schempp''' (born '''Ellory Schempp''', August 5, 1940) is an American [[physicist]]<ref name="the kid">{{cite web | url=https://news.tufts.edu/magazine/fall2007/features/the_kid.html| title=The Kid Who Didn't Stand | work=Tufts Magazine | publisher=Tufts University | date=Fall 2007 | accessdate=March 5, 2022| author=Solomon, Stephen D. }}</ref> and the primary student involved in the landmark 1963 [[United States Supreme Court]] decision of ''[[Abington School District v. Schempp]]''<ref name="A V. S">{{cite web | url=https://www.oyez.org/cases/1960-1969/1962/1962_142 | title=ABINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT v. SCHEMPP | accessdate=September 1, 2013}}</ref> which declared that required public school sanctioned Bible readings were unconstitutional.

==Biography==

Schempp was born in [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania|Philadelphia]] and grew up in the Roslyn community of [[Abington Township, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania|Abington Township]]. He graduated from [[Abington Senior High School|Abington High School]] in 1958, and attended [[Tufts University]] where he earned [[bachelor degree]]s in [[physics]] and [[geology]].<ref name="the kid" /> In 1967, Schempp received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physics from [[Brown University]].<ref name="AARP">{{cite web | url=http://www.aarp.org/politics-society/history/info-06-2011/ellery-schempp-where-are-they-now.html | title=Ellery Schempp and the School Prayer Supreme Court Decision | publisher=AARP | date=June 17, 2011 | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | author=Bennett, Kitty}}</ref>

In 1977, Schempp was part of the Pittsburgh Explorer's Group Nanga Parbat Expedition which was to be the first American group to reach the peak of [[Nanga Parbat]] in [[Pakistan]].

Schempp, who is retired, currently resides in [[Boston, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://articles.philly.com/2013-08-07/news/41135503_1_school-principal-readings-ellery-schempp | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130818214427/http://articles.philly.com/2013-08-07/news/41135503_1_school-principal-readings-ellery-schempp | url-status=dead | archive-date=August 18, 2013 | title=Student's simple stand made history | publisher=The Inquirer | date=August 7, 2013 | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | author=Matza, Michael}}</ref>

Stephen D. Solomon, a professor at [[New York University]], has written a book about Schempp and the Supreme Court case entitled ''Ellery’s Protest: How One Young Man Defied Tradition and Sparked the Battle over School Prayer''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gvpt.umd.edu/lpbr/subpages/reviews/solomon0609.htm |title=Ellery's Protest |publisher=Michigan Press |date=2009 |accessdate=September 1, 2013 |author=Solomon, Stephen |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131221152807/http://www.gvpt.umd.edu/lpbr/subpages/reviews/solomon0609.htm |archivedate=December 21, 2013 }}</ref>

==Activism==
{{Main|Abington School District v. Schempp}}
On November 26, 1956, Schempp staged a protest against the school requiring that each student read 10 Bible passages and the [[Lord's Prayer]] each day during [[Homeroom#United States|homeroom]]. That day he brought a copy of the [[Qur'an]] and read from it;<ref name="the kid" /><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2013/06/50-years-after-i-abington-v-schempp-i-a-dissenter-looks-back-on-school-prayer/276921/|title=50 Years After Abington v. Schempp, a Dissenter Looks Back on School Prayer|first=Linda K.|last=Wertheimer|publisher=The Atlantic|date=June 17, 2013|accessdate=December 12, 2022}}</ref> for this he was sent to the principal's office. With the help of his father, Edward Schempp, and the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], they sued the Abington School district over their policy of mandatory Bible readings.<ref name=" AARP" />

To maintain standing in the case, Schempp (and later his younger siblings Roger and Donna) continued to fight this policy in the courts over several years. The Schempps were [[Unitarian Universalist]]s, a theologically liberal religious community. The case was eventually decided in Schempps's favor by the Supreme Court in 1963, five years after he had graduated from high school.<ref name="A V. S" /> The precedent that this decision established, that the public school does not have the right to sponsor religious exercises and then pressure students to take part in them has appeared time and time again in every church-state case focusing on religion in public schools.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.au.org/church-state/may-2013-church-state/featured/ellerys-epic-exploit | title=Ellery's Epic Exploit | publisher=American's United | date=May 2013 | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | author=Boston, Rob | archive-date=February 26, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170226122854/http://www.au.org/church-state/may-2013-church-state/featured/ellerys-epic-exploit | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Schempp considers himself to be an atheist,<ref name=" AARP" /> but supports the [[Unitarian Universalist]] organizations and is a strong supporter of the [[ACLU]] and of the separation of church and state. He is a popular speaker at Unitarian Universalist and [[Secular humanism|secular humanist]] meetings, where he speaks about his landmark protest as well as the current state of democracy, the [[United States Constitution|Constitution]], and the [[United States Bill of Rights|Bill of Rights]]. As of 2011, he was still active in the Bedford Unitarian Universalist church near his home.<ref name=" AARP" />

Schempp is a member of the [[American Humanist Association]], the [[Freedom from Religion Foundation]], and [[Americans United for the Separation of Church and State]]. In 1996, he received the Religious Liberty Award from Americans United. In 2005, he received the Humanist Religious Liberty Award from AHA.<ref>{{cite web |title=Annual Humanist Awards |url=https://americanhumanist.org/awardees/ |website=American Humanist Association |publisher=American Humanist Association |access-date=3 June 2026}}</ref> He is on the advisory board of the [[Secular Student Alliance]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.secularstudents.org/advisory_board#ellery |title=Advisory Board to the SSA |publisher=SSA website |accessdate=September 1, 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130901054018/http://www.secularstudents.org/advisory_board |archivedate=September 1, 2013 }}</ref> and the [[Secular Coalition for America]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.secular.org/bios/Ellery_Schempp.html | title=SCA Advisory Board Biography | publisher=Secular.org website | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807022713/https://secular.org/bios/Ellery_Schempp.html | archive-date=August 7, 2013 | url-status=dead }}</ref> He has traveled throughout the country talking about his experiences.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://lowcountryhumanists.org/SEPS/sep-2005-11.pdf | title=A personal experience | publisher=Low Country Humanists | date=November 2005 | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | archive-date=March 4, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304050318/http://lowcountryhumanists.org/SEPS/sep-2005-11.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.uuworld.org/ideas/articles/3063.shtml | title=A victory for the heretics | publisher=uuworld.org | date=January–February 2003 | accessdate=September 1, 2013 | author=French, Kimberly}}</ref>

In 2002, Schempp was elected to Abington Senior High School's hall of fame for his accomplishments in physics. In his acceptance speech, he said that "When I left Abington in 1958, it wasn’t clear that Abington ever wanted to see me again". The award did include the notation “Initiated school prayer suit against Abington which was eventually decided by U.S. Supreme Court in 1963.”<ref name="the kid" /><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2013/06/50-years-after-i-abington-v-schempp-i-a-dissenter-looks-back-on-school-prayer/276921/|title=50 Years After Abington v. Schempp, a Dissenter Looks Back on School Prayer|work=The Atlantic|date=June 17, 2013|first=Linda K.|last=Wertheimer|access-date=March 5, 2022}}</ref>

==Physics==

Schempp's [[doctoral thesis]] was entitled ''Nuclear Quadrupole [[Resonance]] in [[Nitrogen]] Heterocycles''. This work was the precursor to the development of [[magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI) on which he continued to work for a substantial portion of his career.<ref name=" the kid" />
